You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Gospel

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching, 'Gospel' (Greek: euangelion, 'good news') primarily denotes the announcement of salvation accomplished by God through Jesus Christ — specifically his death for sins, burial, resurrection, and lordship — offered to all who believe. It is understood less as a symbol than as a proclamation: the message that in Christ, God has acted decisively to redeem humanity, forgive sin, and inaugurate his kingdom.",

    "1 Corinthians 15:1-4 (Paul's summary definition: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised)",

    "Mark 1:1 ('The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God')",
    "Mark 1:14-15 (Jesus proclaiming the gospel of God: 'the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel')",
    "Isaiah 52:7 and Isaiah 61:1 (the herald of good news, cited as Old Testament background)",
    "Luke 4:18-19 (Jesus applying Isaiah's good-news commission to himself)",
    "Galatians 1:6-9 (there is one true gospel that must not be distorted)",
    "Matthew 28:18-20 and Mark 16:15 (the commission to proclaim the gospel to all nations)",
    "Ephesians 1:13 ('the gospel of your salvation')"
  ],

      "meaning": "The gospel as the announcement of the kingdom of God — the in-breaking reign of God inaugurated in Jesus' ministry, not only the transaction of individual forgiveness. Emphasized in the Synoptic Gospels and in much modern scholarship (e.g., N.T. Wright, kingdom-centered readings).",

    },

      "basis": [
        "Mark 1:1 (as a title)",
        "Early church usage (Justin Martyr, Irenaeus) rather than a proof text"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The gospel as a counter-imperial proclamation: euangelion deliberately echoes Roman imperial announcements (e.g., the 'good news' of Caesar's accession), so declaring Jesus as Lord is a political-theological challenge to empire. A significant strand in modern academic interpretation.",

      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {

    {
      "meaning": "'Full gospel' or prosperity-oriented readings in which the good news includes guaranteed physical healing, material blessing, and success in this life. Held in some Pentecostal/charismatic and prosperity-teaching circles; widely rejected by mainstream theology as a distortion.",

        "Isaiah 53:5 with 1 Peter 2:24 (healing in the atonement)",

    {
      "meaning": "Liberationist readings in which the gospel is centrally good news to the poor and oppressed — social, economic, and political liberation as intrinsic to the message (liberation theology, social gospel movement).",

  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "'Gospel' is one of the most stable terms in Christian vocabulary. There is broad ecumenical consensus — Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and evangelical — that it means the good news of salvation in Christ's death and resurrection, with 1 Corinthians 15:1-4 and Romans 1:16 as the standard defining texts. Disagreements are mostly about scope and emphasis (kingdom vs. individual salvation, spiritual vs. social dimensions) rather than about the core referent. The literary sense ('a Gospel' = one of the four books) is a distinct but universally recognized secondary usage. Prosperity and strictly political readings exist but are contested and not part of the mainstream consensus."
}

However, “Gospel” is primarily a theological and literary term rather than a fixed biblical symbol, and traditions differ over whether its central emphasis is Christ’s saving work, the kingdom of God, personal salvation, ecclesial teaching, or social restoration."

BOOK ENTRY
The gospel of the coming kingdom, in which the law goes forth from Zion — proclaimed beforehand to Abraham and at Mount Sinai, and renewed under Jesus' rule.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: the good news that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Gen 12:3; Isa 52:7; 2:3; Jer 31:33; Gal 3:8; Heb 4:2) · see Gospel, ch. 5

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Genesis 12:3 — And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.
Isaiah 52:7 — How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!
Isaiah 2:3 — And many people shall go and say, Come ye, and let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths: for out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.
Jeremiah 31:33 — But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
Galatians 3:8 — And the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the heathen through faith, preached before the gospel unto Abraham, saying, In thee shall all nations be blessed.
Hebrews 4:2 — For unto us was the gospel preached, as well as unto them: but the word preached did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
